I have farmed these lands in Quzhou County for nearly four decades, and I know what works here. The North China Plain gives us two crops a year if you manage the calendar right: winter wheat followed by summer maize. That is what I will stick with this year. My family has about six mu of good irrigated land, and at my age I do not want to gamble on new crops like vegetables or cotton that need more labor and carry price risk. The wheat is already in the ground—I sowed it last October after rotary tillage. Now it is greening up, so I will top-dress it and irrigate three or four times through jointing and grain filling. For the summer maize, I will plant a hybrid variety like Nongda 372 right after the wheat harvest in early June, using no-tillage direct seeding into the wheat stubble to save time and fuel. I use improved seeds and standard compound fertilizers because the yields are reliable and the grain dealers come right to the village. I will keep pesticide sprays to what is necessary—about four times for the wheat and three for the maize—to control aphids, weeds, and the occasional fungus when the weather turns humid.
